concept.name: Three inside down
concept.definition: A three-candlestick bearish reversal pattern introduced by Gregory Morris as a confirmed bearish harami: a long white body in an uptrend is followed by a small black body contained within it (the harami), and then a third candle closing below the second candle's close. The third candle's lower close is the confirmation that distinguishes it from the unconfirmed two-candle harami.
concept.intuition: First the rally stalls inside the prior big candle, then the next candle actually closes lower, confirming that sellers, not buyers, won the standoff.
concept.mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long white body; candle 2 is a black (non-doji) body engulfed by body 1; candle 3 closes below candle 2's close (many implementations require a black body). Shadow lengths are disregarded; a close of candle 3 below candle 1's close is considered stronger confirmation.
concept.formula: Three inside down when C1 > O1 (long body), O2 < C1, C2 > O1, min(O2, C2) > O1, max(O2, C2) < C1, and C3 < C2.
concept.failure_modes: Even with the built-in confirmation, many instances fail in strong uptrends where the dip is immediately bought. Empirical frequency-efficiency statistics (e.g., CandleScanner on S&P 500 data) show only moderate predictive power.
concept.misconceptions: It is not any three declining candles; the first two must form a genuine bearish harami with the second body inside the first. It is a modern formalization by Morris, not a classical Japanese pattern.
concept.example: After a rally, a stock prints a long white candle (60.00 to 63.00), a small black candle inside it (62.50 to 61.70), then a third candle closing at 61.20, below the second close. The three inside down confirms the harami as a bearish reversal signal.
